subject: english
title: KS2 English diagnostic
curriculum: National Curriculum in England, key stage 2 English programme of study (2013), with the Year 6 SATs reading and grammar, punctuation and spelling strands

skills.name: Finding information
skills.why: Finding the right details in a text is the first step in understanding it, and a big part of the Year 6 reading test.
skills.strong: {name} reads carefully and finds the right details quickly.
skills.developing: {name} finds most details but sometimes misses one or answers from memory instead of checking.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet finding details in a text reliably. Every reading task builds on this, so it comes first.
skills.next_step: We will practise skimming, scanning and checking answers against the text.

skills.name: Inference and understanding
skills.why: Working out what a writer suggests, not just what they say, carries the most marks in the Year 6 reading test.
skills.strong: {name} reads between the lines well and explains characters' feelings and motives.
skills.developing: {name} follows what happens but finds it harder to explain what is suggested, or to back it up with evidence.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet confident working out what a text suggests. This matters more every year, so it is worth building now.
skills.next_step: We will talk through small details in short texts and practise backing up answers with evidence.

skills.name: Vocabulary and language
skills.why: Understanding word meanings, and why a writer chose them, helps with reading and makes writing richer.
skills.strong: {name} works out word meanings well and understands why writers choose particular words.
skills.developing: {name} knows many words but finds it harder to work out new ones from the text around them.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet confident working out what words and phrases mean in a text. This holds back understanding in every subject, so it is worth real focus.
skills.next_step: We will build vocabulary through reading together and practise using clues in the text to work out meanings.

skills.name: Grammar and punctuation
skills.why: Grammar and punctuation make writing clear to the reader, and they have their own test in Year 6.
skills.strong: {name} uses and recognises grammar and punctuation accurately.
skills.developing: {name} knows the basics but is less sure with apostrophes and with terms such as adverbs and clauses.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet secure with grammar and punctuation. This affects all writing, so it is worth securing now.
skills.next_step: We will teach one grammar or punctuation point at a time, with short practice and lots of examples.

skills.name: Spelling and writing
skills.why: Accurate spelling and well-built sentences let children show what they know in every subject.
skills.strong: {name} spells well and writes clear, well-punctuated sentences.
skills.developing: {name} writes with good ideas but makes spelling errors with harder words and word endings.
skills.gap: {name} is not yet spelling common words and patterns reliably. This affects writing in every subject, so it is worth steady practice.
skills.next_step: We will practise spelling patterns little and often and write short pieces together, checking as we go.

passages.title: The Lighthouse
passages.text:
Maya had never liked the dark. So when Aunt Ros said the power had gone off across the whole island, Maya pulled her blanket right up to her chin.

"Don't look so worried," Aunt Ros laughed, holding up a heavy iron key. "The old lighthouse has its own lamp. Somebody needs to light it, and tonight that somebody is us."

The wind howled as they hurried along the cliff path. Rain stung Maya's cheeks, and the sea below crashed against the rocks like an angry giant. At the top of the lighthouse, one hundred and twelve steps later, Aunt Ros struck a match with trembling fingers. Nothing happened. She tried again. Still nothing.

"Let me," said Maya quietly. She cupped her hands around the tiny flame, just as she had seen her grandad do on camping trips. The wick caught, flickered, and then burst into a bright, steady glow.

Far out at sea, a small fishing boat had been searching for the harbour. Its crew saw the beam sweep across the waves, and they turned for home.

Back at the cottage, Aunt Ros made two mugs of hot chocolate. "You know," she said, "I think you're braver than you think."

Maya looked out at the lighthouse, still shining through the storm. For the first time she could remember, the dark did not seem quite so dark.

passages.title: Lights That Keep Sailors Safe
passages.text:
For hundreds of years, lighthouses have helped ships find their way at night and in bad weather. They are built on coasts, cliffs and rocky islands, where the sea is most dangerous.

Each lighthouse has its own pattern of flashes, called its 'character'. By counting the flashes, sailors can tell exactly which lighthouse they are looking at, and so work out where they are.

In the past, every lighthouse had a keeper who lived there and kept the lamp burning all night. It was a lonely job. Today, almost all lighthouses in the UK work automatically, and engineers visit a few times a year to check them.

Many lighthouses are painted with bright stripes. This helps sailors to recognise them in the daytime, too.

questions.ref: KS2 reading 2b: retrieve and record information
questions.stem: How many steps are there to the top of the lighthouse?
questions.explain: 'one hundred and twelve steps later'. The number is written in words, so the child has to convert it.

questions.ref: Y2: use question marks and capital letters
questions.stem: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
questions.explain: A question starts with a capital letter and ends with a question mark.

questions.ref: KS2 reading 2a: give the meaning of words in context
questions.stem:
'The wind howled as they hurried along the cliff path.'

Which word could replace 'howled' without changing the meaning much?
questions.explain: 'Howled' describes a loud, wild noise, so 'roared' is closest. 'Whispered' is the opposite.

questions.ref: Y3/Y4 statutory spelling list
questions.stem: Which word is spelt correctly?
questions.explain: 'Friend' is a common exception word: the 'ie' is not sounded as it is written.

questions.ref: KS2 reading 2d: make inferences from the text
questions.stem: Why does Maya pull her blanket up to her chin at the start of the story?
options: She is scared of the dark
She is hiding from Aunt Ros
questions.explain: 'Maya had never liked the dark. So when ... the power had gone off' links the blanket to her fear. 'Cold' is a guess not supported by the text.

questions.ref: KS2 reading 2b: retrieve and record information from non-fiction
questions.stem: In 'Lights That Keep Sailors Safe', what is a lighthouse's 'character'?
options: The person who looks after it
The island it is built on
questions.explain: 'Each lighthouse has its own pattern of flashes, called its character.' The everyday meaning of 'character' (a person) is the trap.

questions.ref: Y2/Y3: identify word classes (verbs)
questions.stem:
Which word is the verb in this sentence?

The waves crashed against the rocks.
questions.explain: 'Crashed' is the action, so it is the verb. 'Waves' and 'rocks' are nouns and 'against' is a preposition.

questions.ref: Y2: add -es to nouns ending in consonant + y
questions.stem: Which is the correct spelling of more than one 'baby'?
questions.explain: For a word ending in a consonant then y, change the y to i and add -es: babies.

questions.ref: KS2 reading 2g: explain how meaning is enhanced through choice of words and phrases
questions.stem:
'the sea below crashed against the rocks like an angry giant'

What does this comparison suggest about the sea?
options: It is loud, powerful and frightening
It is a long way away
questions.explain: An angry giant is huge, loud and scary, so the simile shows the sea is powerful and frightening in the storm.

questions.ref: KS2 reading 2d: infer characters' feelings
questions.stem:
Aunt Ros 'struck a match with trembling fingers'.

What does this suggest about her?
questions.explain: Trembling fingers suggest she is cold from the rain or nervous, even though she seemed confident earlier. The correct option covers both readings.

questions.ref: KS2 reading 2b: retrieve and record information
questions.stem: What did Maya do to help the lamp light?
options: She cupped her hands around the flame
She fetched a new box of matches
She asked her grandad to help
questions.explain: 'She cupped her hands around the tiny flame.' Grandad is only mentioned as the person she learned it from.

questions.ref: Y3/Y4: apostrophes for possession and contraction
questions.stem: Which sentence uses an apostrophe correctly?
options: Maya's aunt lives by the sea.
questions.explain: 'Maya's aunt' shows possession. 'Boy's' should be 'boys' (a plural), 'dogs' needs 'dog's', and 'Its'' should be 'It's'.

questions.ref: KS2 reading 2a: give the meaning of words in context
questions.stem:
'Today, almost all lighthouses in the UK work automatically.'

What does 'automatically' mean here?
options: By themselves, without a person working them
questions.explain: The next part of the sentence says engineers only visit a few times a year, which shows nobody needs to work the lamp. 'By hand' is the opposite.

questions.ref: KS2 reading 2g: explain how meaning is enhanced through choice of words
questions.stem:
'The wick caught, flickered, and then burst into a bright, steady glow.'

Why has the writer used three verbs one after another?
options: To show the flame growing step by step
To slow down a sad moment
questions.explain: Caught, flickered, burst: each verb is a stage, so the reader watches the flame grow from nothing to a strong light.

questions.ref: KS2 reading 2d: explain and justify inferences with evidence
questions.stem: Why does Aunt Ros say, 'I think you're braver than you think'?
options: Maya climbed the steps faster than her
Maya was not scared of the storm at all
Maya rowed out to rescue the boat
Maya lit the lamp despite fearing the dark
questions.explain: Maya is afraid of the dark but still lit the lamp in a storm. 'Not scared at all' misses the point that bravery means acting despite fear.

questions.ref: KS2 reading 2b: retrieve information; check statements against a text
questions.stem: According to 'Lights That Keep Sailors Safe', which TWO statements are true?
options: Every UK lighthouse still has a keeper living in it
Sailors count the flashes to tell which lighthouse they can see
Lighthouses are only useful in the daytime
Bright stripes help sailors recognise lighthouses in the daytime
questions.explain: Paragraph 2 describes counting flashes, and the last paragraph describes the stripes. Keepers were in the past, and engineers visit only a few times a year.

questions.ref: Y5: use relative clauses beginning with who, which, where, when, whose, that
questions.stem: Which sentence contains a relative clause?
options: The boat, which had been lost, turned for home.
After the storm, the boat turned for home.
The boat turned for home and the crew cheered.
questions.explain: 'which had been lost' is a relative clause adding information about the boat. 'After the storm' is a fronted adverbial, and the last sentence joins two main clauses with 'and'.

questions.ref: KS2 reading 2d/2h: make inferences; comment on how meaning is enhanced
questions.stem:
The story ends: 'For the first time she could remember, the dark did not seem quite so dark.'

What has changed for Maya?
options: The power has come back on
She feels less afraid because of what she has done
questions.explain: The lighthouse is 'still shining through the storm', so nothing outside has changed. What has changed is how Maya feels after her brave act.

questions.ref: Y5/Y6 statutory spelling list
questions.stem: Which word is spelt correctly?
questions.explain: Necessary has one c and a double s ('one collar, two sleeves').

questions.ref: KS2 writing: composition, sentence structure and punctuation
questions.stem:
Imagine you are Maya. Write 3 to 5 sentences describing the walk to the lighthouse in the storm.

Use at least one joining word such as 'because', 'when' or 'although'. Spend about 6 minutes on this.

rubric.criterion: Describes the storm or the walk with at least one well-chosen detail or sense (sound, feeling, sight)
Written as Maya, in the first person, and the events make sense
Uses a subordinating conjunction (because, when, although, if, as) correctly
Accurate spelling and sentence punctuation (capital letters and full stops) in most sentences

questions.explain: One mark per strand. Be generous with ideas and strict with sentence punctuation. For Year 3 and 4, simple joining words like 'when' and 'because' earn the conjunction mark.
